figures.name: Basil the Great
figures.dates: c. 330 to 379 (died 1 January 379 by the traditional reckoning; some scholars prefer 377 or 378)
figures.places: Caesarea in Cappadocia (born, bishop 370 to 379); studied at Caesarea, Constantinople and Athens; toured the monks of Egypt, Palestine, Syria and Mesopotamia; lived as a monk at Annesi on the river Iris in Pontus (modern central Turkey)
figures.role: Bishop of Caesarea, monastic founder and rule-writer, builder of a hospital and poorhouse, theologian of the Holy Spirit
figures.status_note: Saint in the Orthodox, Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran churches; Doctor of the Church (Catholic); one of the Three Holy Hierarchs (Orthodox, with Gregory of Nazianzus and John Chrysostom). Never condemned. Cautions: several letters under his name are not his (Letter 8 is usually given to Evagrius, Letter 38 perhaps to Gregory of Nyssa, the letters to Apollinarius are doubtful, Letter 46 To a Fallen Virgin is disputed). Much of his strict teaching (the Rules on laughter, slaves and property) was written for monks and nuns, not for the laity; say so wherever it is used.
figures.hook: When the emperor's prefect threatened him with confiscation, exile, torture and death, Basil answered that a man who owns only rags and a few books cannot be robbed, that all the earth is God's, and that death would only send him to God sooner.

stories.story: The prefect Modestus, sent by the Arian emperor Valens to make Basil conform, threatened him with every penalty. Basil said none of them could touch him. Modestus said no one had ever spoken to him like that; Basil replied that perhaps he had never met a bishop. Modestus went back and told the emperor they had been beaten.
stories.source: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43 (Funeral Oration on Basil), sections 48 to 51

stories.story: He built a 'new city' outside Caesarea (later called the Basileias): a hospital, poorhouse and lodging where lepers were nursed. Gregory says Basil, noble-born, kissed the lepers and greeted them as brothers.
stories.source: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43, sections 63 and 64

stories.story: In a famine he gathered the starving of every age, collected food, set out basins of soup and, with his own servants, waited on them himself, like Christ washing feet.
stories.source: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43, sections 35 and 36

stories.story: A newly widowed woman of high birth, pressed into a forced marriage by a judge's assessor, fled to the altar. Basil protected her. The official had Basil's cloak torn off and threatened to flay him; Basil said the combs would cure his liver. The city's arms-factory and weaving-shed workers rioted, and Basil ended up rescuing the man who had insulted him.
stories.source: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43, sections 56 and 57

stories.story: He came home from the universities 'puffed up beyond measure with the pride of oratory'. His older sister Macrina took him in hand until he gave up the fame of speaking for a life of manual work and gave away his property.
stories.source: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina (tr. W. K. Lowther Clarke, 1916), section headed 'Basil returns from the University'

stories.story: At Athens he and Gregory of Nazianzus were inseparable students who knew only two roads, to church and to their teachers, and skipped the feasts and theatres. Gregory later wrote that they seemed to have one soul in two bodies.
stories.source: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43, sections 19 to 21

stories.story: To strengthen his side in a church-boundary quarrel he made his best friend Gregory bishop of Sasima, a dusty, noisy staging post. Gregory never took it up and never quite forgave him.
stories.source: Gregory of Nazianzus, Letter 48 and Oration 43, section 59

temperament.trait: Stern, reserved, often taken for proud
temperament.evidence: Gregory answers those who 'charge him with pride and haughtiness' that what they call pride is 'the firmness and steadfastness and stability of his character', and says 'His very smile often amounted to praise, his silence to rebuke'.
The Modestus exchange: 'Death is my benefactor, for it will send me the sooner to God'.
From his first hermitage he wrote that he had left the town but 'I have not yet been able to get quit of myself', like a seasick traveller who is sick in the big ship and the small boat alike.
One coat, a worn cloak, a bed on the bare ground, vigils, 'his unwashedness', bread and salt; he was chronically ill (the liver joke to the official).
temperament.source: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43, sections 57 and 61

temperament.trait: Quick to take offence with friends
temperament.evidence: When Gregory proposed a meeting with Basil's rival, Basil sent a stiff letter; Gregory replied: 'How hotly and like a colt you skip in your letters.'
'He was puffed up beyond measure with the pride of oratory' (his brother's words).
temperament.source: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina

temperament.trait: Warm and witty in private, by his closest friend's account
temperament.evidence: 'Who was more kindly in his stories, more refined in his wit, more tender in his rebukes?'

genuine_lines.quote: Whose feet then wilt thou wash ? Whom wilt thou care for? In comparison with whom wilt thou be last if thou livest by thyself?
genuine_lines.work: The Longer Rules
genuine_lines.location: Rule 7 (on living with others rather than alone)
genuine_lines.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke, The Ascetic Works of Saint Basil (SPCK, 1925); the archive.org text is OCR and prints a space before the first question mark

genuine_lines.quote: We have not lost the lad; we have restored him to the Lender.
genuine_lines.work: Letter 5, To Nectarius (on the death of his son)
genuine_lines.translation: B. Jackson, NPNF second series vol. 8 (1895), as on New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: For me grass is grass; plant, fish, wild beast, domestic animal, I take all in the literal sense.
genuine_lines.work: Hexaemeron, Homily 9
genuine_lines.translation: B. Jackson, NPNF second series vol. 8 (1895), as on New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: I carry my own troubles with me, and so everywhere I am in the midst of similar discomforts. So in the end I have not got much good out of my solitude.
genuine_lines.work: Letter 2, To Gregory
genuine_lines.translation: B. Jackson, NPNF second series vol. 8 (1895), as on New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Why, perhaps, said Basil, you have not met with a Bishop
genuine_lines.work: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43 (Basil's words to the prefect Modestus, as reported by his friend)
genuine_lines.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as on New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Death is my benefactor, for it will send me the sooner to God, for Whom I live, and exist, and have all but died, and to Whom I have long been hastening.
genuine_lines.work: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43 (Basil to Modestus, as reported)
genuine_lines.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as on New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: So we, if wise, shall take from heathen books whatever befits us and is allied to the truth, and shall pass over the rest.
genuine_lines.work: Address to Young Men on the Right Use of Greek Literature
genuine_lines.translation: F. M. Padelford, Essays on the Study and Use of Poetry by Plutarch and Basil the Great (Yale, 1902)

genuine_lines.quote: Harshness is ever to be put aside, even in censuring.
genuine_lines.work: Letter 2, To Gregory
genuine_lines.translation: B. Jackson, NPNF second series vol. 8 (1895), as on New Advent

misattributed.line: O God, enlarge within us the sense of fellowship with all living things, our brothers the animals... (the 'Prayer of St Basil for animals')
misattributed.truth: Not found in any liturgy, homily or letter of Basil. The wording closely follows prayers in Walter Rauschenbusch's Prayers of the Social Awakening (1910), blended with a First World War prayer for horses. Do not use.

misattributed.line: The bread you store up belongs to the hungry; the coat hanging in your closet belongs to the naked; the shoes rotting in your closet belong to the barefoot; the money in your vaults belongs to the destitute.
misattributed.truth: Genuine in substance: Basil's Homily 6, on 'I will pull down my barns' (Luke 12:18), section 7. But this popular English wording is a loose modern rendering (there are no closets or vaults in the Greek), and no pre-1929 English translation of that homily was found. If used, quote a checked rendering from the Greek (PG 31), not this version.

opinions.position: Living alone is spiritually dangerous. Only in community can you serve, be humbled, be corrected and use your gifts for others.
opinions.side_note: Against the solitary life, for life together. This is his LATER view (the Longer Rules as we have them date from the 370s). Around 358, in Letter 2, he had praised solitude (next entry). A real change of mind.
opinions.quote: Whose feet then wilt thou wash ? Whom wilt thou care for? In comparison with whom wilt thou be last if thou livest by thyself?
opinions.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke, The Ascetic Works of Saint Basil (1925); OCR text
opinions.today: Genuinely split. Many people today prize time alone, introverts especially, and 'I can be spiritual on my own' is common; others, and most church traditions, say faith is lived with people. A strong, clean quiz statement: 'You grow more with people around you than you do alone.'

opinions.position: Earlier view: withdrawal from society stills the passions and lets the mind rise to God.
opinions.side_note: Pro-solitude. His EARLY view (Letter 2, about 358, written from his first retreat in Pontus). Even here he admits he carries his troubles with him. He later argued for community.
opinions.quote: Now solitude is of the greatest use for this purpose, inasmuch as it stills our passions, and gives room for principle to cut them out of the soul.
opinions.translation: B. Jackson, NPNF second series vol. 8 (1895), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Split, as above. Use only to show his change of mind, not as his settled position.

opinions.position: Christians should read pagan (secular) literature, but like bees: take what is true and good and leave the rest.
opinions.side_note: Pro-learning, with discernment. In Letter 223 he also said he had wasted his youth on 'the wisdom made foolish by God' (next entry), so he is for secular learning as a tool, not as a prize.
opinions.quote: So we, if wise, shall take from heathen books whatever befits us and is allied to the truth, and shall pass over the rest.
opinions.work: Address to Young Men on the Right Use of Greek Literature
opinions.translation: F. M. Padelford (1902)
opinions.today: Most people today agree with reading widely, but a real minority of Christians (homeschool and separatist circles) avoid secular books and media; and many secular people would reject any filtering at all. Moderately useful.

opinions.position: Looking back, the years he spent winning a secular education were largely vanity; the Gospel showed him what mattered.
opinions.side_note: A personal regret about his own schooling, not a ban on learning. Pair it with the Address above.
opinions.quote: Much time had I spent in vanity, and had wasted nearly all my youth in the vain labour which I underwent in acquiring the wisdom made foolish by God.
opinions.translation: B. Jackson, NPNF second series vol. 8 (1895), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Plenty of people today feel their degree was wasted time; plenty would call that anti-intellectual. Better as colour for his portrait than as a statement.

opinions.position: A Christian aiming at perfection should own no more than one garment and give the rest away through the church.
opinions.side_note: Radical renunciation, at least for those seeking perfection. This is Letter 150, which Basil wrote in the name of Heraclidas, reporting 'the very godly bishop' (Basil himself), so it is his own teaching in his own composition.
opinions.quote: what he said about poverty was this, that the rule ought to be that every one should limit his possessions to one garment.
opinions.work: Letter 150, To Amphilochius in the name of Heraclidas
opinions.translation: B. Jackson, NPNF second series vol. 8 (1895), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Almost no one today, Christian or not, would sign up for one garment; but 'owning much is a spiritual danger' splits people well. Use the milder form.

opinions.position: Charity needs judgement: give to real need, not to everyone who asks. Better to give through experienced people who can tell the difference.
opinions.side_note: For discerning, organised giving over handing money to every beggar. Same letter as above.
opinions.quote: For he said that experience was needed in order to distinguish between cases of genuine need and of mere greedy begging.
opinions.work: Letter 150, To Amphilochius in the name of Heraclidas
opinions.translation: B. Jackson, NPNF second series vol. 8 (1895), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Strongly split and very everyday: some people give to anyone who asks on the street (and Chrysostom would side with them), others give only through charities that check need. Excellent quiz material, and it sets Basil against Chrysostom.

opinions.position: Killing in war is not murder, as earlier Fathers held, but it still stains the hands; a soldier who has killed should keep away from communion for three years.
opinions.side_note: Middle position: war is permitted, yet killing in it needs repentance.
opinions.quote: Homicide in war is not reckoned by our Fathers as homicide; I presume from their wish to make concession to men fighting on behalf of chastity and true religion. Perhaps, however, it is well to counsel that those whose hands are not clean only abstain from communion for three years.
opinions.translation: B. Jackson, NPNF second series vol. 8 (1895), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Split in an interesting way: most people accept just war; very few think a soldier needs penance afterwards, yet 'moral injury' in veterans is now widely discussed. A subtle, good statement: 'Even a justified killing leaves something to repent of.'

opinions.position: For the believer there is never a time for laughter, because so many are dead in sin and should be mourned. (Elsewhere he allows 'a cheerful smile' but not loud, shaking laughter.)
opinions.side_note: Also bears on 'enjoyment'. Written for monks. In Longer Rule 17 he says a cheerful smile is not unseemly but loud laughter shows a lack of self-control.
opinions.quote: Since the Lord condemns those that laugh it is obvious that there is never a time of laughter for the believer, especially when there is so great a multitude of those who by transgression of the law dishonour God and are dead in sins, for whom one should mourn and grieve.
opinions.location: Rule 31 ('Must we not laugh at all?')
opinions.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke (1925); OCR text
opinions.today: One-sided today: nearly everyone thinks laughter is good. That makes it a vivid 'sparring partner' line rather than a fair statement; if used, soften to 'A serious person should rarely laugh out loud', which some people do still hold.

opinions.position: Medicine is God's gift and should be used; refusing it on principle is contentious, but putting all your hope in doctors is also wrong.
opinions.side_note: Middle position between faith-only healing and trust in medicine alone. Contrast his sister Macrina, who refused a doctor out of modesty and prayed.
opinions.quote: So also in the case of medicine, it is wrong to slander God’s gift because of the evil use made of it.
opinions.location: Rule 55 ('Whether the use of medical remedies is consistent with the ideal of piety')
opinions.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke (1925); OCR text
opinions.today: Most people agree medicine is good; the split is over how much to trust doctors versus prayer, natural remedies or one's own judgement. A second line from the same rule sharpens it: 'While to avoid entirely the benefit of medicine shows a contentious spirit.'

opinions.position: Even when someone breaks God's commands, the right response is pity and sympathy, not anger. Better never to give way to anger at all.
opinions.side_note: Against anger, even 'righteous' anger at sin (in this rule). His Homily Against Anger (no pre-1929 English found) allows anger aimed at the devil and sin.
opinions.quote: if he would avenge a transgression of the Lord’s commandments, there is need not of wrath, but of pity and sympathy
opinions.location: Rule 29 ('How can a man avoid anger?')
opinions.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke (1925); OCR text
opinions.today: Split. Many people today defend anger at injustice as healthy and necessary; others say anger always does harm. The Address to Young Men has the short form: 'for it is much better not to give way to anger at all.'

opinions.position: Music shapes the soul. Avoid songs that stir base passions; use music that calms and improves, as David's harp did for Saul.
opinions.side_note: For careful choice of music, not against music. He also defended new-style antiphonal night psalm-singing against critics in Neocaesarea (Letter 207).
opinions.quote: On the other hand, we must employ that class of music which is better in itself and which leads to better things, which David, the sacred psalmist, is said to have used to assuage the madness of the king.
opinions.work: Address to Young Men on the Right Use of Greek Literature
opinions.translation: F. M. Padelford (1902)
opinions.today: Split. Many people think music is just taste and has no moral effect; others (parents, some churches) believe some music really does harm. Good quiz material: 'The music you listen to changes who you are.'

opinions.position: Defended the new practice of antiphonal psalm-singing through the night against clergy who said it was an innovation; custom is not the test, agreement with the wider Church is.
opinions.side_note: For new forms of worship when they match the wider Church.
opinions.quote: The customs which now obtain are agreeable to those of all the Churches of God.
opinions.work: Letter 207, To the Clergy of Neocaesarea
opinions.translation: B. Jackson, NPNF second series vol. 8 (1895), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Very live today (worship wars over contemporary music, Latin Mass and so on). Split. Basil is on the side of the new style here.

opinions.position: Refuse to watch buffoons and bodies that stir lust, and shut your ears to corrupting songs.
opinions.side_note: Against entertainment that inflames the passions.
opinions.quote: to refuse to feast the eyes on the senseless antics of buffoons, or on bodies which goad one to passion, and to close one's ears to songs which corrupt the mind.
opinions.work: Address to Young Men on the Right Use of Greek Literature
opinions.translation: F. M. Padelford (1902)
opinions.today: Split: many would say what you watch is your own business and does no harm; many Christians and some others avoid explicit shows. Usable.

opinions.position: Nature should fill you with such wonder that the smallest plant reminds you of its Maker.
opinions.side_note: Creation as a constant pointer to God.
opinions.quote: I want creation to penetrate you with so much admiration that everywhere, wherever you may be, the least plant may bring to you the clear remembrance of the Creator.
opinions.translation: B. Jackson, NPNF second series vol. 8 (1895), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Most believers agree, and many non-believers feel awe at nature without thinking of a maker. One-sided among Christians; it splits believers from secular people rather than among Christians.

opinions.position: Read the creation account plainly. He rejects allegorists who turn water, plants and animals into symbols.
opinions.side_note: The literal side, against Origen-style allegory (for the Genesis creation account at least; elsewhere he reads Scripture morally and spiritually too).
opinions.quote: For me grass is grass; plant, fish, wild beast, domestic animal, I take all in the literal sense.
opinions.translation: B. Jackson, NPNF second series vol. 8 (1895), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Strongly split today (literal and symbolic readings of Genesis). Excellent quiz material. Note he is also not interested in the earth's shape ('the servant of God, Moses, is silent as to shapes'), so do not recruit him for either side of modern science debates.

opinions.position: Grave sinners can be restored after penance, and what counts is the sincerity of the repentance, not just the length of time served.
opinions.side_note: For second chances, through real penance. He also refuses fellowship with those who will not change.
opinions.quote: I do not decide such matters absolutely by time, but I give heed to the manner of penance.
opinions.translation: B. Jackson, NPNF second series vol. 8 (1895), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Most people agree that sincere change matters more than time served; the split is about whether serious wrongdoers should ever be fully restored (to jobs, to church roles). Moderately useful.

opinions.position: Never lie; speak the truth in everything.
opinions.side_note: The strict side: no lies at all. (The Address to Young Men also refuses 'the art of lying' in court and business.)
opinions.quote: That one must not lie but must speak the truth in everything.
opinions.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke (1925); OCR text
opinions.today: Split in practice: most people tell white lies and think some lies are kind or necessary; a minority hold that lying is always wrong.

opinions.position: A second marriage is tolerated with penance; a third is not really marriage at all but 'limited fornication'.
opinions.side_note: Strongly against remarriage, especially a third. He is passing on the Fathers' rule and endorsing it.
opinions.quote: but this is no longer described as marriage at all, but as polygamy; nay rather as limited fornication.
opinions.translation: B. Jackson, NPNF second series vol. 8 (1895), as on New Advent
opinions.today: One-sided today: almost everyone accepts remarriage after a spouse dies. A sparring-partner line, not a fair statement.

opinions.position: Runaway slaves who reach a monastery should be improved and sent back to their masters, as Paul sent Onesimus back; only if the master orders sin should the community shield the slave.
opinions.side_note: Accepts slavery as a social order to be humanised, not abolished. The sentence continues 'to their masters'. (His brother Gregory of Nyssa, by contrast, preached against owning slaves at all.)
opinions.quote: When slaves who are under the yoke flee to the brotherhoods, they should be admonished and made better, and then restored
opinions.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke (1925); OCR text
opinions.today: One-sided today (everyone condemns slavery). Not a quiz statement. Useful only as honest background so the portrait is not a whitewash.

opinions.position: Grief at a death is natural and even right, but reason and the hope of resurrection must steady it; the dead are not lost but given back to God.
opinions.side_note: Grief allowed, then governed by hope.
opinions.quote: We have not lost the lad; we have restored him to the Lender. His life is not destroyed; it is changed for the better.
opinions.translation: B. Jackson, NPNF second series vol. 8 (1895), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many people today feel that 'he is in a better place' consolations cut grief short and prefer grief to run its course; others find them the only comfort. Good quiz material.

opinions.position: When you correct someone, never be harsh; humility and gentleness make the correction land. Sometimes tell a story that lets them judge themselves, as Nathan did with David.
opinions.side_note: Gentle, indirect correction.
opinions.quote: Harshness is ever to be put aside, even in censuring.
opinions.translation: B. Jackson, NPNF second series vol. 8 (1895), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many admire blunt, direct feedback; others prefer gentle correction. Good contrast with Jerome.

opinions.position: Some Christian beliefs and practices come from the written Scriptures and others from unwritten apostolic tradition (signing with the cross, facing east to pray, the words of the Eucharistic prayer), and both have the same force.
opinions.side_note: For unwritten tradition alongside Scripture.
opinions.quote: some we possess derived from written teaching; others we have received delivered to us in a mystery by the tradition of the apostles; and both of these in relation to true religion have the same force.
opinions.translation: B. Jackson, NPNF second series vol. 8 (1895), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Sharply split along church lines: Catholics and Orthodox agree, most Protestants hold Scripture alone. Very usable, but it is theological rather than everyday.

opinions.position: Prayer is no excuse for idleness. Pray while you work, since every time suits prayer.
opinions.side_note: Work and prayer together; against people who skip work 'under pretext of prayers'.
opinions.quote: But for prayer and psalmody, as for many other things, every time is suitable ; so that we praise God with psalms and hymns and spiritual songs while we move our hands in work
opinions.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke (1925); OCR text (note the space before the semicolon in the scan)
opinions.today: Most agree work matters; the split is whether spiritual life needs set-apart time rather than being mixed into work. Mildly useful.

opinions.position: Christians should be modest and submissive to authorities in everything, except where God's cause is at stake; then no threat should move them.
opinions.side_note: Related to 'state-religion': here the state was trying to impose a form of Christianity (Arianism) and Basil refused. Reported by Gregory, who knew him.
opinions.quote: But where the interests of God are at stake, we care for nothing else, and make these our sole object.
opinions.work: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43 (Basil to the prefect Modestus, as reported)
opinions.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Most believers agree in principle; the split is how readily to defy authority (civil disobedience, church and state). Moderately useful.

opinions.position: Care for the body only as far as it serves the soul; perfecting the body while neglecting the soul is like polishing your tools and neglecting your trade.
opinions.side_note: Low priority on the body, beauty and fitness.
opinions.quote: Wherein is there any difference between those who take pains that the body shall be perfect, but ignore the soul, for the use of which it is designed, and those who are scrupulous about their tools, but neglectful of their trade?
opinions.work: Address to Young Men on the Right Use of Greek Literature
opinions.translation: F. M. Padelford (1902)
opinions.today: Split and very current (gym culture, 'the body is a temple', wellness). A good everyday statement: 'Time spent on your body is time taken from your soul.'

sparring.over: Basil made him bishop of Sasima against his will to win a church-boundary dispute; Gregory accused him of treating him as a tool and blamed 'your throne' for lifting Basil above himself
sparring.source: Gregory of Nazianzus, Letters 48, 49 and 50; Oration 43, section 59

sparring.over: His early ascetic mentor turned against him; they split over the divinity of the Holy Spirit and Eustathius spread charges against Basil. Basil broke three years of silence to answer him.
sparring.source: Basil, Letter 223, Against Eustathius of Sebasteia

sparring.with: Pope Damasus and the Western bishops
sparring.over: Their slowness and suspicion in the Eastern church crisis. Basil: 'Really lofty souls, when they are courted, get haughtier than ever' and 'what help can come to us from the frown of the West?'
sparring.source: Basil, Letter 239, To Eusebius of Samosata

sparring.over: When Cappadocia was split in two, Anthimus claimed metropolitan rights over half of Basil's churches; he once blocked Basil's road and seized his mules with an armed band.
They attacked his new style of all-night antiphonal psalm-singing and his monks; he defended both.

sparring.with: The emperor Valens and his prefect Modestus (Arian Christians)
sparring.over: Refused to accept the imperial Arian creed under threat of exile and death
sparring.source: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43, sections 48 to 51

portraits.license: Public domain (faithful reproduction of a 2D public-domain work, per the file page)

figures.name: Gregory of Nazianzus
figures.places: Arianzus near Nazianzus in Cappadocia (born, retired, died); studied at Caesarea in Cappadocia, Caesarea in Palestine, Alexandria and Athens; priest and assistant bishop at Nazianzus; named bishop of Sasima (never served); bishop of Constantinople 379 to 381
figures.role: Theologian of the Trinity, preacher, poet and letter-writer; presided for a time at the Council of Constantinople (381), then resigned
figures.status_note: Saint in the Orthodox, Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran churches; Doctor of the Church (Catholic); called 'the Theologian' in the East; one of the Three Holy Hierarchs. Never condemned. Caution: much of his most personal writing (the long autobiographical poems) has no public-domain English; the orations and a selection of letters are in NPNF.
figures.hook: He was made a bishop three times against his will, never set foot in the one his best friend gave him, and resigned the greatest see in the East with a farewell speech asking to go home to 'my desert, my country life, and my God'.

stories.story: Ordained priest by his father by force, he fled to Basil's retreat in Pontus, then came back and gave a long speech explaining why he ran: he longed for quiet and thought guiding souls 'the art of arts'.
stories.source: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 2 (In Defence of His Flight to Pontus), sections 1 to 7 and 16

stories.story: Basil made him bishop of Sasima, a border waystation, to hold territory in a quarrel with another bishop. Gregory refused to go and wrote Basil a series of hurt, stinging letters.
stories.source: Gregory of Nazianzus, Letters 48 to 50

stories.story: Called to Constantinople when the city was held by the Arians, he preached in a small house-chapel and delivered the Theological Orations there. Made bishop of the city, he presided at the Council of 381, was challenged over the legality of his appointment, and resigned with a farewell oration.
stories.source: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 42 (The Last Farewell)

stories.story: When Basil went off to a rugged hermitage in Pontus and praised it, Gregory wrote back mocking it: a 'mousehole' with grand names, sunless as the land of the Cimmerians, with a river too loud for the psalms.
stories.source: Gregory of Nazianzus, Letter 4

stories.story: After the apostate emperor Julian died, Christians wanted revenge on the pagans who had persecuted them. Gregory told them to forgive: no confiscations, no courts, no exile, no scourges.
stories.source: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 5 (Second Invective against Julian), sections 36 and 37

stories.story: He preached the funeral oration for his brother Caesarius, a court physician who died young, promising not to over-grieve, then admitting in the middle of it that his tears had beaten his philosophy.
stories.source: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 7 (On his brother Caesarius), sections 1 and 6

temperament.trait: Loves quiet; dreads office and public life
temperament.evidence: 'My greatest business always is to keep free from business.'
temperament.source: Gregory of Nazianzus, Letter 49, to Basil

temperament.trait: Sensitive and slow to forget a wound
temperament.evidence: Even in Basil's funeral oration he says the Sasima affair was 'a cause of pain which even time has not obliterated'.
Calls Basil's monastery 'your mousehole with the stately names of Abode of Thought, Monastery, School' and Basil 'my grandiloquent friend and inventor of new names'.
'how can I recall those days without my tears showing that, contrary to my promises, my feelings have overcome my philosophic restraint?'

temperament.trait: Distrustful of church politics; often ill
temperament.evidence: Says he has never seen a council of bishops end well and pleads ill-health: 'I am always on the point of breathing my last'.
temperament.source: Gregory of Nazianzus, Letter 130, to Procopius

temperament.evidence: Of his student years with Basil: 'We seemed to have one soul, inhabiting two bodies.'

genuine_lines.quote: For the guiding of man, the most variable and manifold of creatures, seems to me in very deed to be the art of arts and science of sciences.
genuine_lines.work: Oration 2 (In Defence of His Flight to Pontus)
genuine_lines.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as on New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: My greatest business always is to keep free from business.
genuine_lines.work: Letter 49, To Basil (The Praises of Quiet)
genuine_lines.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as on New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: We seemed to have one soul, inhabiting two bodies.
genuine_lines.work: Oration 43 (Funeral Oration on Basil)
genuine_lines.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as on New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: For that which He has not assumed He has not healed; but that which is united to His Godhead is also saved.
genuine_lines.work: Letter 101, To Cledonius, against Apollinarius
genuine_lines.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as on New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Christ is born, glorify Him.
genuine_lines.work: Oration 38 (On the Theophany, or Birthday of Christ)
genuine_lines.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as on New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Let us become like Christ, since Christ became like us.
genuine_lines.work: Oration 1 (On Easter and his Reluctance)
genuine_lines.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as on New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: They who made the Law were men, and therefore their legislation is hard on women
genuine_lines.work: Oration 37 (On Matthew 19:1-12)
genuine_lines.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as on New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Let us conquer those that have oppressed us, with clemency
genuine_lines.work: Oration 5 (Second Invective against Julian)
genuine_lines.translation: C. W. King, Julian the Emperor (1888), on tertullian.org

misattributed.truth: A modern compression of a genuine line in Letter 101 to Cledonius: 'For that which He has not assumed He has not healed'. Quote the letter, not the slogan.

opinions.position: Education, including pagan literature and science, is the first of human goods; Christians who despise it are boorish and wrong.
opinions.side_note: Strongly pro-learning (more openly than Basil).
opinions.quote: I take it as admitted by men of sense, that the first of our advantages is education; and not only this our more noble form of it, which disregards rhetorical ornaments and glory, and holds to salvation, and beauty in the objects of our contemplation: but even that external culture which many Christians ill-judgingly abhor, as treacherous and dangerous, and keeping us afar from God.
opinions.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Most people agree education is good; the split is among Christians who distrust secular universities. Clean contrast with Tertullian.

opinions.position: Arguing about God is not for everyone, not for every audience, not at every time and not on every point; it needs a purified life and a serious purpose, not gossip after the races.
opinions.side_note: Restrictive: theology is not casual debate.
opinions.quote: Not to every one, my friends, does it belong to philosophize about God; not to every one; the Subject is not so cheap and low; and I will add, not before every audience, nor at all times, nor on all points; but on certain occasions, and before certain persons, and within certain limits.
opinions.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Strongly split: most people today think anyone may question and debate God anywhere (the internet runs on it); a minority think such talk needs reverence and preparation. Excellent quiz material.

opinions.position: Leading and caring for souls is the hardest art there is; a man should hesitate to take church office and must be purified himself before he purifies others.
opinions.side_note: Reluctant about office, not ambitious for it. He fled his ordination.
opinions.quote: A man must himself be cleansed, before cleansing others: himself become wise, that he may make others wise
opinions.work: Oration 2 (In Defence of His Flight to Pontus)
opinions.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Many people agree leaders should get their own lives in order first; many others say you learn by doing and nobody would lead if they waited to be worthy. Usable.

opinions.position: His chief aim was to stay free of business and church politics; if everyone did the same, the Church would have no troubles.
opinions.side_note: Anti-ambition, pro-quiet.
opinions.quote: My greatest business always is to keep free from business.
opinions.work: Letter 49, To Basil (The Praises of Quiet)
opinions.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Split and everyday: ambition and hustle are admired, yet many people long to opt out. A fine quiz statement: 'The best life is one with as little business in it as possible.'

opinions.position: He longed above all for calm and retirement, to close the doors of the senses and speak only to himself and God.
opinions.side_note: Pro-solitude by temperament, though he spent his life in service. Contrast Basil's later rule for community.
opinions.quote: there came over me an eager longing for the blessings of calm and retirement, of which I had from the first been enamoured to a higher degree, I imagine, than any other student of letters
opinions.work: Oration 2 (In Defence of His Flight to Pontus)
opinions.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Split, as with Basil. Gregory and Basil sit on opposite sides here, which is useful.

opinions.position: People need different treatment: some doctrine, some example, some the spur, some the curb. No single method of guidance fits everyone.
opinions.side_note: Tailored correction.
opinions.quote: As then the same medicine and the same food are not in every case administered to men's bodies, but a difference is made according to their degree of health or infirmity; so also are souls treated with varying instruction and guidance.
opinions.work: Oration 2 (In Defence of His Flight to Pontus)
opinions.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Mostly agreed today; the split is 'same rules for everyone' versus 'depends on the person'. Moderately useful.

opinions.topic: new: one standard for men and women
opinions.position: Laws that punish a wife's adultery but excuse a husband's are unjust; men wrote them. God gives one standard to both.
opinions.side_note: For equal sexual morality for men and women, against the Roman double standard.
opinions.quote: I do not accept this legislation; I do not approve this custom. They who made the Law were men, and therefore their legislation is hard on women
opinions.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today agree in principle, though double standards persist in practice. A striking reveal line more than a divisive statement.

opinions.position: One marriage is the law; a second is indulgence; a third is transgression.
opinions.side_note: Against remarriage, but less harsh than Basil's canon.
opinions.quote: The first is law, the second is indulgence, the third is transgression, and anything beyond this is swinish
opinions.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as on New Advent
opinions.today: One-sided today (remarriage is widely accepted). Sparring-partner material only.

opinions.position: Christ, unlike the old law, does not allow divorce for any cause; only adultery allows separation, and in everything else spouses must be patient with each other.
opinions.side_note: Strict on divorce.
opinions.quote: Now the Law grants divorce for every cause; but Christ not for every cause
opinions.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Split: most people accept divorce for many reasons; many Christians still hold that only adultery (or abuse) justifies it. Usable in a softened form: 'Unhappy spouses should usually stay and be patient.'

opinions.position: Keep Christmas without decorating porches and streets, dancing, music, perfumes, rich food and fine clothes; celebrate it spiritually instead.
opinions.side_note: Against festive show and decoration, for a sober feast.
opinions.quote: Let us not adorn our porches, nor arrange dances, nor decorate the streets; let us not feast the eye, nor enchant the ear with music
opinions.work: Oration 38 (On the Theophany, or Birthday of Christ)
opinions.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Wonderful everyday split: many people love decorating for Christmas; others think the decorations and spending bury its meaning. Strong quiz candidate ('Christmas lights and parties miss the point').

opinions.position: Anything beyond what you truly need is excess, especially while others go hungry.
opinions.side_note: Strict on luxury.
opinions.quote: (for to my mind every superfluity is intemperance, and all which is beyond absolute need) — and this while others are hungry and in want, who are made of the same clay and in the same manner.
opinions.work: Oration 38 (On the Theophany, or Birthday of Christ)
opinions.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many think comfort beyond need is fine if earned; others feel guilty spending while others go without. Good.

opinions.position: Baptize babies at once if they are in danger of death; otherwise wait until about age three, when they can answer something about it.
opinions.side_note: A middle way between infant and believer's baptism.
opinions.quote: But in respect of others I give my advice to wait till the end of the third year, or a little more or less, when they may be able to listen and to answer something about the Sacrament
opinions.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Genuinely split among Christians (infant baptism versus believer's baptism); Gregory satisfies neither camp fully. Theological rather than everyday.

opinions.position: There is an unquenchable, eternal fire for the wicked; he notes that some prefer a more merciful reading of that fire, but does not adopt it himself here.
opinions.side_note: Eternal punishment affirmed, with the merciful view mentioned and left open. Contrast Macrina (Gregory of Nyssa's dialogue), who teaches that evil will be wholly destroyed.
opinions.quote: the unquenchable fire which is ranged with the worm that dies not but is eternal for the wicked. For all these belong to the destroying power; though some may prefer even in this place to take a more merciful view of this fire, worthily of Him That chastises.
opinions.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Split today (eternal hell, annihilation, universal hope). Gregory's hedge makes him a poor pole for either side; use Macrina for the hopeful pole.

opinions.position: Assemblies of bishops usually make things worse: love of contention and power, not solutions. The safe course for the soul is to keep quiet.
opinions.side_note: Deep distrust of church meetings and politics (written after the Council of 381).
opinions.quote: For my part, if I am to write the truth, my inclination is to avoid all assemblies of bishops, because I have never seen any Council come to a good end, nor turn out to be a solution of evils. On the contrary, it usually increases them.
opinions.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as quoted at earlychurchtexts.com
opinions.today: Relatable and split: many people think big meetings and committees rarely solve anything; others believe in collective decision-making. A fun, everyday quiz statement.

opinions.position: Mourn the dead, but neither too little nor too much; the law of grief keeps us from both coldness and excess.
opinions.side_note: Measured grief; he admits his own tears overcame his restraint.
opinions.quote: For I am neither going to lament for him who is gone more than is good— as I should not approve of such conduct even in others — nor am I going to praise him beyond due measure.
opinions.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many today think there is no 'too much' in grief; others value composure. Good contrast between Gregory (tears allowed) and Macrina (restraint).

opinions.position: When the tables turn, do not take revenge on those who persecuted you: no confiscations, no lawsuits, no exile, no beatings. Conquer them with clemency.
opinions.side_note: Bears on 'state-religion': Christians newly back in favour should not use state power against pagans.
opinions.quote: Let us conquer those that have oppressed us, with clemency; and above all let humanity be our director
opinions.translation: C. W. King, Julian the Emperor (1888), on tertullian.org
opinions.today: Split: many think wrongdoers should face the courts and justice matters more than mercy; others prefer to let it go. A good quiz statement: 'If someone who hurt you falls into your power, let them go.'

opinions.position: A bishop should not live like a consul, with fine food, clothes, horses and processions; the people want orators and money-managers, but they should want priests.
opinions.side_note: For plain-living clergy.
opinions.quote: For they seek not for priests, but for orators, not for stewards of souls, but for treasurers of money, not for pure offerers of the sacrifice, but for powerful patrons.
opinions.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Most people agree pastors should not live lavishly, yet many churches still choose leaders for speaking and fundraising. Fairly one-sided in principle; strong as a reveal line.

opinions.position: A small faithful flock with no roof but the sky is worth more than grand gilded churches full of wrong belief.
opinions.side_note: Said of the Arians, who held the great churches of Constantinople while his congregation met in a house-chapel.
opinions.quote: not knowing that better is faith, with no other roof but the sky to cover it, than impiety rolling in wealth
opinions.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Split: some love beautiful churches, others think buildings waste money that should go to people. Needs care: his point is about true belief, not architecture as such.

opinions.position: Speak when the Spirit moves you and keep silent when He does not; be neither a chatterer nor needlessly mute.
opinions.side_note: Balanced; he later kept a whole Lent in silence (382).
opinions.quote: I am neither so talkative, as to desire to speak, when He is bent on silence; nor so reserved and ignorant as to set a watch before my lips when it is the time to speak
opinions.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Mostly agreed in principle. Weak as a statement; good as colour.

opinions.position: A homeless foreigner at your door should be welcomed as Christ, who was a stranger for your sake.
opinions.side_note: For hospitality to strangers and foreigners.
opinions.quote: If a stranger fall at your feet, homeless and a foreigner, welcome in him Him who for your sake was a stranger
opinions.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7 (1894), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Personal hospitality is widely admired; it touches the immigration debate, which is sharply split. Keep any statement personal ('I would take a homeless stranger into my home'), not political.

sparring.over: The Sasima appointment: 'I throw the blame on your throne, as having on a sudden lifted you above yourself'; and Basil's touchy letters: 'How hotly and like a colt you skip in your letters.'
sparring.source: Gregory of Nazianzus, Letters 48 and 50; Oration 43, section 59

sparring.over: Whether Christ had a full human mind; Gregory: what He has not assumed He has not healed
sparring.source: Gregory of Nazianzus, Letter 101, To Cledonius

sparring.over: Anthimus tried to win Gregory to his side against Basil, invaded the marshes of Sasima and taunted Gregory with 'Basilism'

sparring.with: The bishops of the Council of Constantinople (381)
sparring.over: His appointment to Constantinople was challenged and his peace policy frustrated; he resigned and afterwards avoided all councils
Their habit of treating theology as a debating sport; the Theological Orations answer them
sparring.source: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 27, sections 1 to 3

portraits.title: Saint Gregory the Theologian, mosaic, Saint Sophia Cathedral, Kyiv
Saint Gregory the Theologian, mosaic in the Palatine Chapel, Palermo
Saint Gregory the Theologian, fresco, Church of the Theotokos Peribleptos, Ohrid

figures.name: Macrina the Younger
also_known_as: 'the Teacher' (Gregory of Nyssa's name for her)
figures.dates: c. 327 to 379 (died 19 July 379, months after Basil)
figures.places: Born in Cappadocia or Pontus; lived all her adult life on the family estate at Annesi on the river Iris in Pontus (modern north-central Turkey), which she turned into a community of women
figures.role: Eldest sister of Basil the Great and Gregory of Nyssa; ascetic and head of a women's community; teacher of her brothers
figures.status_note: Saint in the Orthodox and Catholic churches (feast 19 July). Never condemned. Caution: she left no writings. Everything we have comes from her brother Gregory of Nyssa: the Life of Macrina (a biography by an eyewitness) and On the Soul and the Resurrection, a literary dialogue modelled on Plato's Phaedo in which she is 'the Teacher'. How much of the dialogue is her own words and how much Gregory's is debated. Its teaching that evil will finally be wholly destroyed (the universal restoration) was later associated with Origenism and contested, though Gregory of Nyssa was never condemned. Do not confuse her with Macrina the Elder, her grandmother.
figures.hook: When her fiancé died she refused every other suitor, saying there is one marriage as there is one birth and one death; then she talked her proud brother Basil out of his rhetoric and her wealthy mother into sharing the servants' bread and beds.

stories.story: Betrothed at twelve to a young man who died, she treated the betrothal as a marriage, refused all suitors, and resolved never to leave her mother.
stories.source: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina (tr. W. K. Lowther Clarke, 1916), sections on her betrothal and 'Macrina resolves never to leave her mother'

stories.story: When Basil came home a celebrated speaker, 'puffed up beyond measure with the pride of oratory', she took him in hand until he gave up fame for manual work and poverty.
stories.source: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina, 'Basil returns from the University'

stories.story: She persuaded her mother to live on equal terms with her former slave-girls: same food, same beds, no regard for rank. The household became a community of prayer.
stories.source: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina, 'Mother and daughter make further progress in the ascetic life'

stories.story: When her favourite brother Naucratius was killed in a hunting accident and her mother collapsed, Macrina held herself together and talked her mother through it.
stories.source: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina, 'Macrina the one support of her mother'

stories.story: She had a tumour in her breast but would not let a doctor see her body. She prayed all night, made a salve of the mud from her tears, and asked her mother to trace the cross on it; the tumour vanished, leaving a small scar that her nuns showed Gregory at her death.
stories.source: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina (told to Gregory by the nun Vestiana)

stories.story: In a famine she picked up babies abandoned by the roadside and raised them; at her funeral they mourned her as their mother.
stories.source: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina, account of her funeral

stories.story: Dying of fever, she let her grieving brother Gregory weep for a little, then argued with him for hours about death, the soul and the resurrection, and when he complained of his troubles she scolded him for ingratitude.
stories.source: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina; On the Soul and the Resurrection (opening)

temperament.evidence: Her brother says her determination was more steadfast than could be expected at her age, and that she repelled every suitor with argument.
temperament.source: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina

temperament.evidence: At Naucratius's death she 'both preserved herself from collapse, and becoming the prop of her mother's weakness, raised her up from the abyss of grief'.
temperament.source: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina

temperament.evidence: She deflated Basil's pride and rebuked Gregory: 'Will you not cease to be insensible to the divine blessings?'
temperament.source: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina

temperament.trait: Gentle but firm with grief, like a driver with a bolting horse
temperament.evidence: 'she gave in to me for a little while, like a skilful driver, in the ungovernable violence of my grief; and then she tried to check me by speaking'.
temperament.source: Gregory of Nyssa, On the Soul and the Resurrection, opening

temperament.evidence: She hid her difficult breathing and 'in every way she tried to be cheerful, both taking the lead herself in friendly talk'.
temperament.source: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina

temperament.trait: A reasoner who wants proof from Scripture too
temperament.evidence: In the dialogue she argues step by step and then insists that 'truth is to be found only in that upon which the seal of Scriptural testimony is set'.
temperament.source: Gregory of Nyssa, On the Soul and the Resurrection

genuine_lines.quote: Thou, O Lord, hast freed us from the fear of death. Thou hast made the end of this life the beginning to us of true life.
genuine_lines.work: Her dying prayer, in Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina
genuine_lines.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke (1916), on tertullian.org

genuine_lines.quote: Will you not cease to be insensible to the divine blessings? Will you not remedy the ingratitude of your soul?
genuine_lines.work: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina (her words to Gregory)
genuine_lines.location: 'Gregory returns to Macrina, who recalls the events of her childhood' (PG 46.982B)
genuine_lines.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke (1916), on tertullian.org

genuine_lines.quote: Why, what is the special pain you feel, asked the Teacher, in the mere necessity itself of dying? This common talk of unthinking persons is no sufficient accusation.
genuine_lines.work: Gregory of Nyssa, On the Soul and the Resurrection
genuine_lines.translation: W. Moore and H. A. Wilson, NPNF second series vol. 5 (1893), as on New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: But He that becomes all things will be in all things too; and herein it appears to me that Scripture teaches the complete annihilation of evil.
genuine_lines.work: Gregory of Nyssa, On the Soul and the Resurrection (Macrina speaking)
genuine_lines.location: on 1 Corinthians 15:28, late in the dialogue
genuine_lines.translation: W. Moore and H. A. Wilson, NPNF second series vol. 5 (1893), as on New Advent

misattributed.line: Lines and deeds of Macrina the Elder (her grandmother, a confessor under persecution who handed on the teaching of Gregory the Wonderworker)
misattributed.truth: Often confused online. Macrina the Younger is the granddaughter; the persecution story and the Gregory the Wonderworker link belong to the grandmother.

misattributed.line: Any 'saying of St Macrina' quoted as her own writing
misattributed.truth: She wrote nothing that survives. Every line comes through Gregory of Nyssa, and the dialogue On the Soul and the Resurrection is his literary composition in her voice. Attribute as 'Macrina, in her brother Gregory's account'.

opinions.position: There is only one marriage in a life, as there is one birth and one death; her dead fiancé was not dead but absent, so she would not marry another.
opinions.side_note: Against remarriage, in the strongest form (even after a betrothal). Reported speech.
opinions.quote: she would say that it was absurd and unlawful not to be faithful to the marriage that had been arranged for her by her father, but to be compelled to consider another; since in the nature of things there was but one marriage, as there is one birth and one death.
opinions.work: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina
opinions.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke (1916), on tertullian.org
opinions.today: One-sided in its strict form; but 'there is one great love in a life' is a real romantic belief many people hold. Usable softened: 'If the person you loved died, you would not look for another.'

opinions.position: Rank and wealth mean nothing among believers: she had her mother live with the former slave-girls as sisters, sharing food, beds and everything.
opinions.side_note: Also 'wealth'. Radical equality inside the household.
opinions.quote: She induced her to live on a footing of equality with the staff of maids, so as to share with them in the same food, the same kind of bed, and in all the necessaries of life, without any regard to differences of rank.
opinions.work: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina
opinions.location: 'Mother and daughter make further progress in the ascetic life' (PG 46.970C)
opinions.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke (1916), on tertullian.org
opinions.today: Most people agree in principle that people are equal; few live it (eating and living with the people who work for you). A good sharp statement: 'I would live exactly as the people who work for me live.'

opinions.position: Fame won by eloquence is empty; she drew Basil from pride in his rhetoric to poverty and work with his hands.
opinions.side_note: Against learning as a path to fame, not against learning itself (she was learned in Scripture). Reported deed, not her words.
opinions.quote: Nevertheless Macrina took him in hand, and with such speed did she draw him also toward the mark of philosophy that he forsook the glories of this world and despised fame gained by speaking, and deserted it for this busy life where one toils with one's hands.
opinions.work: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina
opinions.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke (1916), on tertullian.org
opinions.today: Split: many admire brilliant speakers and careers; many think manual, humble work is more honest. Good for a statement like 'A job with your hands is better for the soul than a job that makes you admired.'

opinions.position: Christians should not grieve for the dead as those without hope; she let her brother weep for a while, then reasoned him out of it. She taught her nuns that the one right time for tears is prayer.
opinions.side_note: Restrained grief, governed by hope and reason. Stricter than Gregory of Nazianzus.
opinions.quote: She quoted the Apostle's words about the duty of not being grieved for them that sleep; because only men without hope have such feelings.
opinions.work: Gregory of Nyssa, On the Soul and the Resurrection
opinions.translation: W. Moore and H. A. Wilson, NPNF second series vol. 5 (1893), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Split, as with Basil's letter: many today resist being told to stop grieving; others find hope the true comfort. Good quiz statement.

opinions.position: Anger, desire and fear are not the soul itself but growths attached to it, like warts; they can be conquered, and when turned toward good they become praiseworthy (Daniel's desire, Phinehas's anger).
opinions.side_note: Passions are not our true self; master them and redirect them.
opinions.quote: But, whenever their impulse is towards what is noble, then they become matter for praise, as his desire did to Daniel, and his anger to Phineas, and their grief to those who nobly mourn.
opinions.work: Gregory of Nyssa, On the Soul and the Resurrection
opinions.translation: W. Moore and H. A. Wilson, NPNF second series vol. 5 (1893), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Strongly split: modern culture often says your feelings are who you are and should be expressed; Macrina says they are not your true self. A second line from the same passage is more vivid: 'yet they are not the soul , but only like warts growing out of the soul's thinking part' (note the space before the comma in the source).

opinions.position: In the end God will be all in all and evil will be completely destroyed; nothing will be left outside the good.
opinions.side_note: The hopeful pole: universal restoration. Caution: these are Gregory of Nyssa's words in her voice.
opinions.quote: But He that becomes all things will be in all things too; and herein it appears to me that Scripture teaches the complete annihilation of evil.
opinions.work: Gregory of Nyssa, On the Soul and the Resurrection
opinions.translation: W. Moore and H. A. Wilson, NPNF second series vol. 5 (1893), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Split today: many ordinary people hope everyone ends up with God; many Christians hold to eternal hell. Strong statement.

opinions.topic: new: punishment after death as cleansing
opinions.position: The fire after death purifies rather than simply punishes; it lasts as long as there is evil to burn, so each person's suffering matches the evil in them.
opinions.side_note: Remedial, proportional punishment. Related to 'universal-salvation'.
opinions.quote: That, said the Teacher, is my meaning; and also that the agony will be measured by the amount of evil there is in each individual.
opinions.work: Gregory of Nyssa, On the Soul and the Resurrection
opinions.translation: W. Moore and H. A. Wilson, NPNF second series vol. 5 (1893), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Split: Catholics (purgatory) and universalists lean yes; many Protestants say no; many non-religious people find the idea of fair, finite punishment appealing.

opinions.position: Dwelling on your troubles is ingratitude; count what God has given you and the prayers that carried you.
opinions.side_note: Gratitude over complaint.
opinions.quote: Will you not cease to be insensible to the divine blessings? Will you not remedy the ingratitude of your soul?
opinions.work: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina
opinions.location: her words to Gregory on the eve of her death (PG 46.982B)
opinions.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke (1916), on tertullian.org
opinions.today: Split: many think venting is healthy and 'just be grateful' is dismissive; others think complaining is a bad habit. Very everyday and personal; strong quiz material.

opinions.position: Christ has freed us from the fear of death; the end of this life is the beginning of true life.
opinions.side_note: No fear of death.
opinions.quote: Thou, O Lord, hast freed us from the fear of death. Thou hast made the end of this life the beginning to us of true life.
opinions.work: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina (her dying prayer)
opinions.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke (1916), on tertullian.org
opinions.today: Split: many people, believers included, admit they fear death; others say they do not. Good personal statement: 'I am not afraid to die.'

opinions.position: She trusted prayer and the sign of the cross for healing rather than letting a doctor examine her, judging exposure of her body worse than the pain; she was healed.
opinions.side_note: Also 'new: medicine': contrast her brother Basil's rule that refusing medicine outright is contentious. Her motive was modesty, not a theory against doctors. Her mother argued the other way ('the medical art... was sent from God').
opinions.quote: she said it would suffice for the cure of her disease if her mother would make the holy seal on the place with her own hand.
opinions.work: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina
opinions.location: the nun Vestiana's account of the scar (PG 46.992B)
opinions.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke (1916), on tertullian.org
opinions.today: Split: most people go to the doctor; some Christians pray first and trust healing; modesty about medical exams is a real concern for some. Handle with care: never present as advice to skip medical care.

opinions.position: She chose to stay home and serve her widowed mother rather than leave, and made the family home itself her life's work.
opinions.side_note: Family duty and calling combined, not in conflict.
opinions.quote: she settled on one safeguard of her good resolution, in a resolve not to be separated from her mother even for a moment
opinions.work: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina
opinions.location: 'Macrina resolves never to leave her mother' (PG 46.964D)
opinions.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke (1916), on tertullian.org
opinions.today: Split: many think adult children should leave home and make their own lives; others (and many cultures) honour staying to care for parents. Good personal statement.

opinions.topic: new: Scripture as the test of reasoning
opinions.position: Reason carefully, but hold as true only what Scripture confirms.
opinions.side_note: Reason under Scripture.
opinions.quote: And who, she replied, could deny that truth is to be found only in that upon which the seal of Scriptural testimony is set?
opinions.work: Gregory of Nyssa, On the Soul and the Resurrection
opinions.location: on the passions (reply to Gregory's request for scriptural proof)
opinions.translation: W. Moore and H. A. Wilson, NPNF second series vol. 5 (1893), as on New Advent
opinions.today: Split between Bible-first believers and people who trust reason or experience first. Usable, though somewhat theological.

sparring.over: His pride in rhetoric and fame when he came home from Athens; she won
sparring.source: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina

sparring.over: His grief at Basil's death and his doubts about the soul's survival: the whole dialogue is their argument; also his complaints about his troubles. A family debate, not a public clash.
sparring.source: Gregory of Nyssa, On the Soul and the Resurrection; Life of Macrina

sparring.over: Whether to see a doctor about her tumour (the mother said medicine was sent from God; Macrina refused out of modesty and prayed)
sparring.source: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina
